1345.title: The blessing
1345.hook: the service ends in a blessing, often Numbers 6:24–26
1345.howItsDone: Christian services often end with a benediction: the minister or priest raises a hand or both hands over the congregation and speaks a blessing, often Numbers 6:24–26 or 2 Corinthians 13:14, sometimes with the sign of the cross, followed by a dismissal such as "go in peace."

segments.voice: Yesterday, the offering: a basket on a pole, bread up the aisle, and David handing back what was handed to him. Your line was all things come of thee.

Coats are half on. The last hymn is over. A toddler is making a break for the door, and someone is checking a phone. Then the minister raises a hand over the room, or both hands, palms out, and the shuffling stops. Heads bow. Into the quiet come words from the book of Numbers: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee." A few more lines, an amen, and the doors open onto the parking lot and the rest of the week. Before anyone reaches the car, something has been spoken over them. Today's word is benediction.

You met these lines on day four hundred three. Today, where they land: at the door. A benediction is a blessing spoken over people, and a service often closes with one. One often used comes from Numbers. God tells Moses to speak to Aaron and his sons: "On this wise ye shall bless the children of Israel." Then: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee: The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee: The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace." Kept, shone upon, given peace. These were Israel's words first, and Jews pray them still. Notice who is blessing. The next verse says the priests "shall put my name upon the children of Israel; and I will bless them." The raised hands pass the blessing on; in the text, God is the one who blesses. In Leviticus, after the offerings, "Aaron lifted up his hand toward the people, and blessed them." Near the end of Luke, out near Bethany, Jesus "lifted up his hands, and blessed them. And it came to pass, while he blessed them, he was parted from them." Their last sight of him is a blessing in progress. Churches end in different ways. Some use Numbers. Some use Paul: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all." Some add the sign of the cross. And often, a few last words: go in peace.

Lift one hand a little, palm out, toward one person heading into a hard day: a friend before a test, a parent in a hospital. If you pray, say the old words over them, one line per breath: the LORD bless thee, and keep thee; the LORD make his face shine upon thee; the LORD give thee peace. If you don't, wish them those three things your own way.
Benediction. A blessing spoken over people, often the words from Numbers, spoken as people leave.
Your line: go in peace. The room empties into the week, blessed. See you tomorrow.

1346.title: Weddings
1346.hook: vows before God and witnesses: for better, for worse
1346.howItsDone: Christian couples exchange vows in church before a minister or priest and the congregation as witnesses; Catholics celebrate marriage as a sacrament, the Orthodox crown the couple in the service of crowning, and Protestant churches hold a service of worship honoring marriage as holy, without counting it a sacrament.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the blessing, and the word benediction: hands raised over a room, and people sent out the door. Your line was go in peace.

"Dearly beloved, we are gathered together here in the sight of God, and in the face of this congregation." That's how the old English prayer book opens a wedding. In front, two people who barely slept. Beside them, a best man patting his pocket for the third time to check the rings. In the second row, a grandmother crying since the processional. In a few minutes, two people will say, in front of all of them, that they'll stay through the good years and the terrible ones. Today: weddings.

Day two hundred heard Jesus on marriage; today, the wedding itself. A Christian wedding is a promise made in two directions at once: to each other, and before God. Start with the witnesses: "in the sight of God, and in the face of this congregation." The people in the pews aren't an audience. They're there to see the promise, and remember it. Then the vows. In the prayer book, each promises "to have and to hold from this day forward, for better for worse, for richer for poorer, in sickness and in health, to love and to cherish, till death us do part." Those words come from the prayer book, not the Bible. And they name the worse before it arrives. Nobody knows what's coming; the vow says yes anyway. Genesis says a man will "leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh," and in Matthew, Jesus quotes it. In John, Jesus is at a wedding in Cana when the wine runs out, and John calls what he does there the beginning of his miracles. Some couples choose Ruth's promise, "whither thou goest, I will go," which in the story Ruth says to Naomi, her mother-in-law. Churches differ. Catholics call marriage a sacrament, and in Catholic teaching the bride and groom are its ministers: they marry each other, and the priest witnesses. The Orthodox call it a holy mystery, and crowns are placed on, or held over, the couple's heads. Protestant churches that keep two sacraments, baptism and the Lord's Supper, honor marriage as holy without counting it a third.

1347.title: Ordination
1347.hook: hands laid on, and prayer for the Spirit
1347.howItsDone: In Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches, a bishop ordains deacons, priests and bishops by laying on hands with prayer; other Protestant churches ordain ministers with the laying on of hands by other ministers or elders; Quakers do not ordain.

segments.voice: Yesterday, weddings: vows made in the face of the congregation, naming the worse before it comes. Your line was for better, for worse.

Nobody in the church moves. At the front, a person in a plain white robe kneels on the stone floor, head bowed. The bishop places both hands on that head. Then, one after another, others come and add their hands, on the head, on the shoulders, until a small crowd of palms rests on one person. The silence stretches. Then a prayer goes up, asking the Holy Spirit to come on the one kneeling there. When the person stands, the robe is the same. For the church, something has changed.

Ordination is how a church sets someone apart for ministry, and at its center is a very old gesture: hands laid on, with prayer. It runs all through Acts. First, helpers in Jerusalem. The apostles need people to look after the widows' daily food, and the church chooses some: "when they had prayed, they laid their hands on them." Prayer first, then hands. Second, a sending. In Antioch, the church is worshipping and fasting, and the Holy Spirit says, "Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them." Then, "when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away." Barnabas and Saul are already among that church's teachers. The hands don't keep them; they send them off. Third, a gift that needs tending. Paul tells Timothy: "Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery." And in a second letter: "stir up the gift of God, which is in thee by the putting on of my hands." Stir it up, the way you'd stir a fire burning low. Fourth, where churches differ. Catholics and Orthodox call holy orders a sacrament: bishops ordain deacons, priests and other bishops, and they see a line of laid-on hands reaching back to the apostles. Anglicans keep bishops too. Other Protestant churches ordain ministers with hands laid on by other ministers or elders. Quakers ordain no one. Churches also differ on who may be ordained. Where they do ordain, hands and prayer tend to be at the center, as in Acts.

Bring to mind your pastor, priest or minister, or, if you don't have one, someone who has cared for your spirit another way: a teacher, a grandparent, a friend who listens. Picture your hand resting lightly on their shoulder. If you pray, ask God to stir up the gift in them; if you don't, simply wish them strength for the work.
Ordination. A church setting someone apart for ministry, with hands and prayer for the Spirit, then sending them out.
Your line: hands laid on. Hands that send out, not hands that keep. Until tomorrow.

1348.title: Anointing the sick
1348.hook: oil and prayer for the sick (James 5:14)
1348.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the anointing of the sick as a sacrament for those seriously ill or frail with age; the Orthodox celebrate Holy Unction, in some parishes for all the faithful during Holy Week; some Protestant churches anoint with oil when elders pray for the sick, and others lay on hands and pray.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ordination: hands laid on with prayer, and teachers sent away. Your line was hands laid on.

A small metal case, the size of a lipstick. Inside, a pad of cotton soaked in olive oil. A priest carries it in a jacket pocket down a hospital corridor, into a room where a man lies with a drip in his arm. Across the city, a grocery-store bottle of olive oil sits on a coffee table. A few friends from church gather around a woman in an armchair. One puts a dab of oil on her forehead with a thumb, and they begin to pray. Different rooms, the same two things. Today's word is unction.

Day one hundred fifty-four paired confession with healing oil; today, the oil. Unction means an anointing with oil, and for the sick the instructions come from James: "Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord: And the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up; and if he have committed sins, they shall be forgiven him." The sick person calls. The church comes. Oil and prayer go together. First, the oil was ordinary. In Mark, the disciples anoint "with oil many that were sick, and healed them." The Good Samaritan bandages a stranger's wounds, "pouring in oil and wine." James puts that kitchen-shelf remedy inside a prayer. Catholics call it the anointing of the sick and count it a sacrament. Once called extreme unction and kept mostly for the dying, it's now offered to anyone facing serious illness, surgery, or the frailty of age. The Orthodox call it Holy Unction, and in some parishes people who aren't bedridden at all come forward to be anointed during Holy Week. Some Protestant churches anoint with oil when elders pray for the sick; others lay hands on the sick and pray without it. Last, the promise: the Lord shall raise him up. Some Christians read that as bodily healing; others hear strength, forgiveness, and company in suffering. Some recover and some don't. The rite says they're not left alone.

Bring to mind one person who is ill right now, in a hospital, at home, or sick in a way nobody can see, and sit as you would in a chair pulled up beside them. If you pray, ask God to raise them up, in whatever way that means for them today. If you don't, keep them company in your mind, the way the elders in James came when called.
Unction. An anointing with oil. For the sick, it's oil and prayer together, brought by the church when someone calls, as in James.
Your line: oil and prayer. The sick call, and the church comes. Go gently.

1349.title: Confession rites
1349.hook: from the Orthodox confession before an icon to the general confession in a prayer book
1349.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians confess before an icon of Christ with a priest beside them; Catholics confess privately to a priest in the sacrament of penance and receive absolution; Anglican, Lutheran and some other Protestant services include a general confession said together, followed by a declaration of forgiveness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, unction: a little case of oil, a hospital corridor, and the elders coming when called. Your line was oil and prayer.

In a small Orthodox church, a woman stands at a lectern near the front, facing an icon of Christ, with a Gospel book and a cross resting there. The priest stands beside her, not across from her. She speaks quietly. When she's finished, she bows her head, and he lays the end of his stole over it and prays. Across town, in a church with a prayer book in every pew, a whole congregation kneels, and every voice says the same words at once: "We have left undone those things which we ought to have done."

Christians confess in different rooms, leaning on the same two lines. The first comes one verse after yesterday's oil: "Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed." In James, confession is spoken out loud to another person. The second is from the first letter of John: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." Now, three rooms. First, the Orthodox. The person confessing stands before an icon of Christ, the priest beside them, and in some Orthodox prayers before confession the priest describes himself as only a witness: it's Christ who hears and forgives. Second, the Catholic sacrament of penance, often called reconciliation. A person tells their sins to a priest in private, behind a screen or face to face, and hears the words of absolution. The priest is bound by the seal of confession: he may never repeat what he heard. Third, the general confession, said together from the old English prayer book: "We have left undone those things which we ought to have done; And we have done those things which we ought not to have done." Some Protestant services include a prayer of confession like it, followed by words of forgiveness. Notice the order: left undone comes first, the good nobody got around to, the visit, the apology, the help. In every room the shape is the same. Say it out loud. Hear that it's forgiven.

Don't make a list; look for just one thing, something you did, or, following the prayer book, something you left undone: the call you didn't make, the thank-you never said. Name it plainly to yourself, without excuses and without piling on. If you pray, bring it to God and rest on John's promise, faithful and just to forgive; if you don't, let it be named, and notice what changes when it is.
Confession rites. The church's ways of saying sin out loud and hearing it forgiven: before an icon, to a priest, or all together.
Your line: we have left undone. The good undone gets named first. See you tomorrow.

1350.title: Vows
1350.hook: monks and nuns vow poverty, chastity and obedience, or stability
1350.howItsDone: Catholic monks, nuns, friars and sisters profess vows such as poverty, chastity and obedience, and Benedictines vow stability, conversion of life and obedience, after a long period of testing; Orthodox monastics and some Anglican and Lutheran communities also take vows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, confession rites: before an icon, to a priest in private, or a whole room kneeling. Your line was we have left undone.

A man in a plain black habit stands at the altar of a monastery church. In front of his brothers, he signs a sheet of paper he has written out by hand and lays it on the altar. Then he lifts his arms and sings a single line from the Psalms, asking God to uphold him so that he may live, and not be put to shame in his hope. The monks sing it back, and again. Then he lies down on the floor while they pray. When he gets up, he belongs to that community for good. Today: vows.

A vow is a promise made to God, out loud, meant to be kept, and some Christians make vows that shape their whole lives. Start with a story. In Matthew, a rich young man asks Jesus what he still lacks, and Jesus answers: "If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me." The young man goes away sorrowful. But according to his biographer Athanasius, a young Egyptian named Antony heard that same verse read in church, gave away his land, and began a life of prayer. Next, what they vow. In Catholic religious life the classic vows are poverty, chastity and obedience: owning nothing of your own, not marrying, and listening for God's will through the community and its leaders. Benedictines, following the Rule of Saint Benedict, vow stability, staying with one community; conversion of life; and obedience. Stability means no running away when the brothers get on your nerves. Orthodox monks and nuns make vows too, and so do some Anglican and Lutheran communities. Then, how seriously. Ecclesiastes warns: "Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay." Communities go slowly too, testing someone a long time before the final vow. Last, how publicly. A psalm says, "I will pay my vows unto the LORD now in the presence of all his people." The paper on the altar says the same. Not a private resolution. A whole life, given wholly, with witnesses.

Say it once, quietly, out loud, so it's a promise and not just a thought. If you pray, make it to God; if you don't, make it to yourself, with this minute as your witness.
Vows. Promises made to God out loud before witnesses, like poverty, chastity and obedience, or stability: a life given over on purpose.
Your line: given wholly. Kept for a day, or kept for life. That's today, done.

1351.title: The basilica
1351.hook: early churches borrowed the Roman hall, a long nave to an apse
1351.howItsDone: Some churches, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant, keep the basilica's long plan: a nave where the congregation gathers and a central aisle leading to the altar or communion table, walked in processions, at weddings and when people come forward to receive communion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vows: a paper laid on an altar, poverty, chastity and obedience, or a Benedictine's stability. Your line was given wholly.

The heavy door swings shut, and the traffic noise is gone. Ahead stretches a long, straight floor. Columns march down both sides in two rows, like trees along a country road. Light falls in from high windows. And far away, at the very end, the wall curves into a half-circle, glowing with gold mosaic, an altar standing in front of it. This room wants anyone in it to go one way: forward. A whole church, shaped like a road. Today: the basilica.

The block turns from rites to spaces, starting with a building borrowed from Rome. First, the hall. Historians describe the Roman basilica as a big public building for law courts and business: a long central hall, columns down each side, and at the far end a rounded space called the apse, where an official sat to hear cases. Second, the choice. When Christians began building large churches, historians point out, they didn't copy the temples around them. A Roman temple was a house for a god's statue, and the crowd mostly stayed outside. Christian worship needed the crowd inside, hearing the word and sharing the table, and the public hall had room. Third, the furniture. The long hall became the nave, where the people stand or sit. In the apse, where an official's seat had been, came the bishop's chair and, before it, the altar. A room built for judgment became a room built for worship, with a table at the end of the road. Fourth, the walk. The shape makes a path, door to altar, and people walk it: in processions, a bride up the aisle, people coming forward to receive communion. The psalms sing that movement: "Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise." And: "I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD." Hebrews uses the same picture for coming near to God: "boldness to enter into the holiest" by "a new and living way." Some churches built since, even ones that look nothing like Rome, still keep the long walk.

segments.voice: Walk slowly to the front of a church, or, if you can't get to one, walk it in your mind: start at the door, one step on each slow breath, no hurry. When you arrive, stand still a moment. If you pray, say the psalm's line, I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD; if you don't, simply stand there and look.

options: They borrowed the Roman basilica, a public hall with room for a crowd to walk to the altar.
